posts.text:
🚨🇺🇸🇮🇷 A US F-35 flashed an emergency code over the Strait of Hormuz and diverted to a UAE base, cause unknown

Start with what's solid. Flight trackers caught the jet sending code 7700, the signal for any emergency from an engine fault to battle damage, before it turned for Al Dhafra.

Nobody has said what went wrong, and earlier CENTCOM flatly denied Iran's claim that it damaged an F-16 on a similar route.

Bobby Jones, a retired Navy commander, isn't calling this a hit either.

His question is why pilots are over Iran so often, and his answer is that thin stocks of long-range missiles are pushing more missions into crewed jets that have to fly inside Iranian radar range.

Bobby on the limits of even the best airframe there:

"And we're quickly finding out that stealth does not mean invisible."

He fears the day a jet doesn't make it home on camera, because the pressure to hit back would drown out restraint in both parties.

The cheapest insurance against that day is to stop flying predictable routes.

US stocks have rarely been this oversold:

The S&P 500 closed the week 4.1 standard deviations below its 50-day moving average, its widest deviation since August 2015.

This also marks its 3rd-largest deviation in at least 20 years.

By comparison, during the 2008 Financial Crisis, the index’s largest deviation from its 50-DMA was 3.6 standard deviations.

Not even the 2020 Pandemic crash saw such extreme oversold conditions, with the S&P 500 falling 3.8 standard deviations below its 50-day moving average in February.

During the 2022 bear market and the April 2025 post-"Liberation Day" selloff, the S&P 500 fell 3.2 and 3.3 standard deviations below its 50-day moving average, respectively.

This has been one of the sharpest market sell-offs in history.
